fetched_contents.text: Enhanced EDCs removal by membrane fouling during the UF process Highlights * • Filtration behavior of synthetic secondary effluent followed cake filtration law. * • Membrane fouling formed by synthetic secondary effluent enhanced EDCs removal. * • Clean and fouled membranes rejected EDCs mainly by adsorption and size exclusion. Abstract In the paper, fouling behavior of a synthetic secondary effluent was explored and influences of membrane fouling and operation pressures (25, 30, 50, and 75 kPa) on rejection of five endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs) (estrone, 17β-estradiol, estriol, 17α-ethynyl estradiol, and bisphenol A) were explored during the membrane filtration process using 100 kDa polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) ultrafiltration (UF) membrane under constant pressure dead-end filtration system. Fouling behavior of humic compounds was found to obey the rule of cake filtration. Fouled UF membrane revealed enhanced EDCs removal rate by 0.0% to 58.3% corresponding to different EDCs. Cakes grew under various pressures had different specific resistances and porosities. Cake formed under 50 kPa had the lowest porosity 56.8% but had the best EDCs removal efficiency, which may be attributed to adsorption and size exclusion. Besides, EDCs revealed different penetration abilities through fouled membrane with E3 being the most easy to flow out. It can be concluded that 50 kPa may be suitable for UF process operation aiming at EDCs removal and appropriate flux. Keywords Endocrine disrupting chemicals ; Ultrafiltration ; Membrane fouling Introduction Sewage recycle is imperative due to shortage and heavy pollution of water source in China and many places in the world. Secondary effluent from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), owing to its huge amount and relatively fine quality, was chosen as a promising source for water reuse. One key issue of water reuse using secondary effluent is safety problem [1], such as chemical safety caused by endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs), which have estrogenic or androgenic activity at environmental concentrations. In order to ensure the safety of reclaimed water, promising technologies should be developed to deal with EDCs. Up to nowadays, there have been many studies on EDCs removal, including physical means, chemical ways and biological methods. Some researchers have studied adsorption of EDCs by activated carbon (AC) and found that AC is pretty effective in removing a wide range of EDCs in lab, pilot and full-scale plants [2]. However, in order to gain fine removal efficiency, adsorption parameters and operational conditions should be strictly controlled [3], [4], and large amount of AC is needed when used in full-scale plants, which is costing. Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs), such as ozonation, were proven to achieve good EDCs removal effect [5], [6], and chemical structure of targeted EDCs as well as oxidant dose may affect oxidation rate [7]. However, active products after oxidation and huge oxidants demand in full-scale plants inhibited wide utilization of AOPs. Biodegradation processes are the most cost-effective processes, but numerous investigations showed that the efficiency of conventional biodegradation processes was not as good as AOPs and varied a lot due to treatment processes of the WWTPs [8]. Membrane process has attracted great concern in wastewater treatment for contaminants removal. Reverse osmosis (RO) and nanofiltration (NF) were reported to be efficient in removing micro-contaminants, such as EDCs [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], while ultrafiltration (UF) and microfiltration (MF) had limited role in EDCs removal due to their big pore sizes [14], [15], but might be more applicable in cooperation with other technologies in treating actual wastewater [16], [17], meaning UF technology has wide application market in advanced secondary effluent treatment. Therefore, a combined UF-O3 process was established aiming at EDCs removal in our group. This paper mainly focused on attributions of UF membrane on EDCs rejection. During the past decades, removal of EDCs via the UF process has started to attract attention. Influence of Ca2 +, pH, and NOM on adsorption of BPA by UF was studied [18]. Results showed that the existence of NOM decreased retention of BPA on UF, because NOM was competitive in relation with BPA on adsorption sites of UF membrane. Impacts of water properties, such as DOC, SUVA, pH, as well as conductivity, on EDCs elimination during the UF process were also explored [13]. Results showed that EDCs retention by UF was obviously governed by hydrophobic adsorption until steady-state came, when size exclusion was dominant. In summary, it can be concluded that research of EDCs removal by the UF membrane is meaningful, as few reports were about influence of secondary effluent caused membrane fouling on EDCs rejection; moreover no study discussed how operation parameters such as applied pressures affected EDCs retention. So that, behavior of EDCs across secondary effluent fouled UF needs to be further studied. In view of previous studies and our survey, humic compounds are the maximum organic parts of secondary effluent. Moreover, humic matter and calcium are the main contributors to fouling during the UF process [19]. So humic substances were chosen as the organic matter for synthetic secondary effluent in this study. Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) UF membrane, because of its excellent chemical resistance and thermal stability, was utilized in this work [20]. As constant pressure stirred dead-end filtration is widely used for studying membrane fouling during UF filtration [21], so this filtration mode was adopted in this experiment. Effective removal of hydrophobic endocrine-disrupting compounds (EDCs) using polyamide nanofiltration (NF) membranes remains a challenge in membrane-based water treatment. A common belief is that the sorption of hydrophobic EDCs is key to their rejection, while high sorption often leads to low rejection. However, this study reported distinct sorption–rejection behavior of EDCs by various chlorinated polyamide membranes. Specifically, the chlorinated NF90 membrane exhibited significantly reduced sorption and, thus, enhanced rejection for EDCs. This is primarily attributed to the enhanced hydrophilic carboxyl groups through chlorination-induced hydrolysis, which can suppress the hydrophobic interactions between the membrane and the EDCs. More interestingly, the chlorinated VNF1 membrane demonstrated higher sorption but also higher rejection of EDCs than that of the virgin membrane. The high sorption can be attributed to the strong hydrophobic interaction between EDCs and the hydrophobic chlorine attached to the membrane. Meanwhile, the large size of chlorine also strengthened membrane size exclusion, thereby enhancing its rejection of EDCs. Such enhanced size exclusion overperformed the impact of increased sorption, thus leading to enhanced rejection. These findings elaborate the existing membrane sorption–rejection framework and offer valuable insights for the rational design of advanced NF membranes aiming for the effective elimination of EDCs in water and wastewater treatment. fetched_contents.text: Enhanced removal of hydrophobic endocrine disrupting compounds from wastewater by nanofiltration membranes intercalated with hydrophilic MoS2 nanosheets: Role of surface properties and internal nanochannels Highlights * • * • The introduction of MoS2 created hydrophilic surface and nanochannels in PA layer. * • The developed membrane simultaneously enhanced permeance and EDCs rejection. * • The selective nanochannels played a more important role in rejecting EDCs. Abstract The presence of endocrine disrupting compounds (EDCs) in water and wastewater poses potential risks on aquatic environment and human health. Conventional polyamide (PA) nanofiltration (NF) membrane showed poor rejection against EDCs due to unfavorable hydrophobic interaction. In this study, we introduced MoS2 nanosheets (NS) to PA NF membrane by pre-deposition before the interfacial polymerization process, creating hydrophilic surface and nanochannels in the PA rejection layer to enhance removal of hydrophobic EDCs from wastewater. Results showed that the MoS2 NS intercalated membrane simultaneously enhanced water permeance and EDCs rejection, with water/EDC selectivity nearly 6 times larger compared to the control. The enhanced EDC rejection was primarily attributed to the suppressed hydrophobic interaction between membrane surface and hydrophobic EDCs, as well as the selective effect by the MoS2 NS-induced nanochannels. Further calculation based on the solution-diffusion theory indicated that for MoS2 NS intercalated membranes the selective nanochannels played a more important role than the hydrophilic surface in impeding the transport of EDCs across the PA layer. The feasibility of the MoS2 NS intercalated PA membrane for EDC removal was also verified using EDC-contaminated real wastewater. The results of this work highlight the potential of using the designed NF membranes for efficient removal of targeted organic micropollutants from water and wastewater. Introduction Trace organic contaminants, such as endocrine disrupting compounds (EDCs), have been frequently detected in municipal and industrial wastewaters [[1], [2], [3]]. They not only present a formidable challenge to aquatic species in the environment, but also cause pollution of drinking water sources, resulting in adverse effects on human health even at very low concentrations ranging from ng/L to μg/L [3,4]. Moreover, exposure to EDCs may severely disrupt the normal functioning of the endocrine system and result in permanent physiologic changes, particularly on foetuses [5,6]. A recent study has shown that early prenatal exposure to EDCs could be associated with lower IQ of children [7]. Nanofiltration (NF) membrane-based separation process has attracting increasing attention in water treatment and wastewater reclamation [8,9]. NF has the potential to selectively remove those emerging EDCs from contaminated water, as the size of most EDCs is within the range of NF's typical molecular weight cut-off (MWCO, 200–1000 Da). However, the EDCs are often neutral and hydrophobic [10], and the unfavorable interaction between the compounds and membrane surface leads to the insufficient rejection of EDCs by NF membrane, especially the widely used polyamide (PA) membranes [[11], [12], [13]]. For example, a low rejection of estrone (~10%–20%) by PA NF membranes was reported [14]. A NF200 commercial membrane showed <50% rejection of bisphenol A [15]. Although the enhanced sorption of EDCs onto membrane surface might increase the initial rejection, the compound can break through the membrane rejection layer after saturation, resulting in a low rejection of EDCs at steady state [16,17]. Therefore, there is a critical need to engineer the rejection layer of NF membrane to achieve favorable removal of EDCs from contaminated water. One strategy for enhancing the rejection of EDCs by NF membrane is hydrophilic surface coating, but the coating often compromises the membrane water permeability [10,16,18]. For NF-based wastewater treatment and reclamation, the water permeability is important, as membranes with high intrinsic water permeability could reduce energy consumption [19,20]. Incorporating nanoparticles (NPs) into the PA active layer, forming the so-called thin-film nanocomposite (TFN) membrane [21,22], may be an attractive route to address the trade-off between water permeability and EDC selectivity. Recently, it has been observed that, interestingly, a proper selection of nanofillers allows formation of hydrophilic selective nanochannels inside PA layer [23]. However, only spherical NPs have currently been used for creating selective nanochannels in the PA layer [24], and more importantly it still remains unknown whether the created nanochannels can increase the EDC rejection by membranes. Moreover, based on the solution-diffusion model [25], both the surface properties and the created nanochannels could significantly affect the transport of EDCs, as the PA surface properties determine the sorption of EDCs while the nanochannels inside the PA rejection layer control the diffusion of EDCs across the membrane. Nevertheless, there is no systematic study to illustrate the role of PA surface properties and internal nanochannels in rejection of EDCs by membranes. We here hypothesized that hydrophilic two-dimensional (2D) nanomaterials could simultaneously induce hydrophilic surface and create selective nanochannels in PA layer. The hydrophilic surface and nanochannels can potentially improve the rejection of EDCs by membranes, without compromising the membrane water permeability. In this work, MoS2 nanosheets (NS) were used as nanofillers in PA to enhance the EDCs rejection performance by NF membranes. Compared with other 2D nanomaterials, MoS2 NS had smooth surface without any oxygenated functional groups, which can reduce the resistance to transport of water molecules [26]. fetched_contents.text: Experimental Evaluation of the Process Performance of MF and UF Membranes for the Removal of Nanoplastics Abstract Despite the high removal ability of the wastewater treatment technologies, research efforts have been limited to the relatively large-sized microplastics, leaving nanoplastics outside the studied size spectrum. This study aims to evaluate the process performance of MF and UF membranes for the removal of single and mixed solutions of polystyrene nanospheres (120 and 500 nm) and BSA. The process performance was evaluated in terms of the rejection coefficient, the normalized flux, and the permeability recovery. The fouling mechanism of these pollutants was studied, evaluating the effect of different membrane materials, membrane pore sizes, and nanoplastic sizes, as well as the synergetic effect of the mixture of foulants. This study was complemented by surface membrane characterization. Polystyrene nanospheres were successfully removed with all the membranes studied, except for the MF membrane that obtained PS 120 nm rejection coefficients of 26%. Single nanoplastic particles were deposited in UF membranes creating a pore blocking and cake layer formation, whilst the nanoplastics of 120 nm were accumulated inside the MF membrane creating an internal pore blocking. In mixed solutions, the BSA acted in two different ways: (i) as a stabilizer, hindering the deposition of nanoplastics and (ii) as a main foulant that caused a substantial flux reduction. Keywords: ultrafiltration membranes, microfiltration membranes, nanoplastics, membrane process performance, BSA, synergetic effect, wastewater treatment 1. Introduction Plastics have the characteristics of being versatile, durable, cheap, and light. Therefore, they have a wide variety of applications in sectors such as medicine, construction, food, and agriculture. In fact, global plastics production increased to 390.7 million tonnes in 2021 [1]. However, due to their intrinsic properties, plastics take a long time to degrade. Consequently, there is an urgent need for efficient plastic waste management avoiding the further deterioration of this serious environmental problem. When plastics are discarded and not properly recycled, plastic waste and their fragments inevitably end up penetrating water bodies. In addition, when these plastic fragments remain in the environment for long periods of time, they break down into micro- (MPs) and nanoplastics (NPs), called secondary micronanoplastics (MNPs). MPs are defined as plastic fragments smaller than 5 mm, and NPs are defined as plastic fragments smaller than 1 μm [2]. On the other hand, primary MNPs are plastic fragments manufactured in micro–nano size, which can also be found in water bodies. Due to their ubiquity, the concern about our exposure to them and their possible health effects has grown in the last few years. Microplastics have been detected in oceans and fresh water as well as in table salt, drinking water, and air, posing an inevitable human exposure risk [3]. Several authors [4,5,6,7] have reported that wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are the major sources of MNPs in freshwaters. Therefore, if they are not effectively removed from wastewater, they are discharged and reintroduced into the environment. Tang et al. [8] recently published a review article analysing numerous papers published in the last 10 years compiling the removal performance of the different stages typically found in WWTPs. In general terms, WWTPs efficiently remove MPs, obtaining removal efficiencies up to 98% and 99%, for primary and secondary treatments, respectively. Despite the high removal ability of secondary treatment technologies such as conventional activated sludge and membrane bioreactors [9], as well as tertiary treatment technologies, such as disc filter (DF), rapid sand filtration (RSF), and dissolved air flotation (DAF) [10], the research efforts have been mainly limited to the quantification of relatively large-sized MPs, leaving small-sized MNPs outside the studied size range [11]. The evaluation of the removal capacity of small-sized MNPs by WWTPs and advanced water treatment technologies has been limited due to the lack of standardized methods for sampling, identification, and quantification of MNPs from wastewater [12]. This is an important bottleneck that hinders a real evaluation of their release into the water bodies from the WWTPs. In general terms, it is well known that WWTPs efficiently remove relatively large MPs, but small-sized MNPs can pass readily through the WWTPs entering the environment. As an example, Wolff et al. [13] identified MPs > 10 μm in a WWTP in Germany, reporting that 95% of MPs in the effluent of the secondary treatment stage were between 10 and 100 μm. Consequently, to truly understand the efficiency of wastewater treatment technologies, it is important to develop new processes capable of capturing, identifying, and quantifying the small-sized MNPs. Considering the small pore size of microfiltration (MF, 0.1–10 μm) and ultrafiltration (UF, 0.01–0.1 μm) membranes, pressure-driven membranes could not only be implemented as a tertiary treatment for the removal of MNPs but also as a sampling and preconcentration of these pollutants [11,14]. The use of MF/UF membranes in concentration mode could also improve the subsequent detection/identification steps of these pollutants, allowing reaching smaller detection and quantification limits. In this context, it is important to conduct studies to understand the process performance of pressure-driven membranes for the separation of MNPs from water matrices, giving special attention to nanoplastics. EDC physicochemistry interacts with membrane transport and adsorption through a combination of molecular weight, hydrophobicity, charge, solubility, and diffusivity effects, and EDC structure determines whether molecules are adsorbed, rejected, or trapped in fouling layers. The evidence supports a non-uniform picture: some EDCs are primarily rejected by pore size, while others are more strongly influenced by adsorption and hydrophobic interactions.

First, molecular weight and hydrophobicity are major determinants of rejection mechanisms. A 2026 study on hydrophobic EDCs in NF membranes reports that sorption and rejection are not simply correlated: hydrophobic EDCs are often strongly adsorbed, yet high sorption can reduce rejection because the compound can later bypass the rejection layer at steady state [N4-F2]. The same study also links rejection to hydrophobic interactions and molecular size, showing that chlorinated membranes can suppress hydrophobic interaction and improve rejection even for hydrophobic EDCs [N4-F2]. A separate 2021 NF membrane study on hydrophobic EDC removal emphasizes that hydrophobic interaction between the membrane surface and EDCs is a major barrier to rejection, while the presence of hydrophilic surface features or internal nanochannels can increase rejection by reducing that interaction and enhancing selective transport control [N4-F3]. These findings suggest that EDCs with higher hydrophobicity are more likely to be adsorbed onto membranes and fouling layers, but their rejection depends on whether they can be excluded by pore size or whether hydrophobic interactions dominate [N4-F2][N4-F3].

Charge is another key factor. The 2026 NF study notes that EDCs exhibit significant correlation with rejection rate when molecular weight (MW), hydrophobicity, and charge are considered together [N4-R5]. That same evidence base supports a broader mechanistic framework in which EDC rejection is driven by size exclusion, electrostatic repulsion, hydrophobic partitioning, adsorption, and other effects [N6-R1]. This means that charged EDCs may be rejected more effectively by electrostatic repulsion or excluded by size, depending on pore size and membrane charge, while uncharged or hydrophobic EDCs may rely more on adsorption and hydrophobic interaction [N6-R1][N4-R5].

Solubility and diffusivity affect transport across different pore sizes. The 2023 NF study on hydrophobic EDC removal states that hydrophobic EDCs are often neutral and hydrophobic [N4-F3], which implies that solubility in water may be low and diffusivity through membrane pores may be limited by hydrophobic mismatch. The same paper explains that EDC rejection is affected by both surface properties and created nanochannels, and that selective nanochannels can impede EDC transport more strongly than hydrophilic surface effects [N4-F3]. The 2025 membrane handbook excerpt also explains that particles are rejected when they are larger than the membrane pore size, and that pore size governs which particles pass through the membrane [N6-R2]. Taken together, these sources suggest that solubility and diffusivity are especially important for small EDCs and for systems where pore size is close to molecular dimensions, because those molecules may enter the membrane and then be rejected by transport limitations, size exclusion, or adsorption in the rejection layer [N6-R2][N4-F3].

EDC structure affects adsorption capacity and fouling propensity. The 2023 NF study highlights that hydrophobic EDCs are often neutral and hydrophobic [N4-F3], and that their removal is limited by unfavorable hydrophobic interaction with the membrane surface [N4-F3]. It also notes that the introduction of hydrophilic surface features and selective nanochannels can reduce hydrophobic interaction and enhance rejection [N4-F3]. Another 2026 NF study similarly reports that chlorinated membranes can suppress hydrophobic interaction and improve rejection, with the chlorinated VNF1 membrane showing higher sorption but also higher rejection because increased sorption can be offset by enhanced size exclusion [N4-F2]. These examples show that EDCs with branched or bulky hydrophobic structures are more prone to adsorption onto membranes and fouling layers, while EDCs with hydrophilic groups or smaller sizes may be rejected more effectively by size exclusion or transported through selective pathways [N4-F2][N4-F3]. The evidence also implies that adsorption capacity and affinity are not fixed across all EDCs; they depend on molecular architecture and the membrane surface chemistry [N4-F2][N4-F3].

Overall, the interaction between EDC physicochemistry and membrane transport/adsorption is best summarized as: hydrophobic and high-molecular-weight EDCs are more likely to be adsorbed and retained by membrane surfaces and fouling layers, while smaller or more hydrophilic EDCs are more likely to be rejected by size exclusion and other transport mechanisms. Charge can further modulate rejection through electrostatic effects, and diffusivity and solubility determine whether EDCs enter the membrane and then exit or become trapped [N4-F2][N4-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2].

Pore size, pore size distribution, and membrane structure together determine transport and rejection by separating solutes by size, controlling solute entry and retention, and influencing retention and fouling through material and surface properties.

First, pore size cutoff and pore size distribution separate solutes by size. The 2026 technical bulletin excerpt explains that particles are rejected if they are larger than the UF/MF membrane pore size, and that the particles are physically unable to fit through [N6-R2]. The same source also suggests that pore size governs which particles pass through the membrane, consistent with the idea that pore size cutoff defines the minimum size of molecules or particles that can cross the membrane [N6-R2]. The 2025 membrane handbook excerpt reinforces this by stating that particles in feed water will be rejected if they are larger than the UF/MF membrane pore size [N6-R2]. The 2023 MF/UF nanosphere study provides experimental evidence that MF membranes reject 120 nm PS nanospheres at only 26% and that UF membranes show different fouling behavior depending on pore blocking and cake layer formation [N5-F4]. This indicates that pore size cutoff is not a simple binary threshold but depends on the membrane’s pore size distribution, the particle size, and the operating conditions.

Pore size distribution also affects how solutes behave. The 2026 study on pore size distribution in UF membranes investigates the impact of different pore size distribution forms on UF membrane performance [N3-R1]. While the evidence here is not detailed enough to specify the exact pore-size-distribution mechanisms, it clearly supports the idea that membrane performance is sensitive to how pore sizes are distributed across the membrane structure [N3-R1]. The 2000 study on determining pore size distributions of UF membranes by model calculations also examines the effects of protein adsorption on membrane transport and notes that different adsorption mechanisms lead to very different behavior [N3-R2]. Although this is more about adsorption than pore size, it shows that membrane structure and transport are closely intertwined, and that pore size distribution can influence how solutes interact with the membrane surface and rejection layer [N3-R2]. The 2024 PMC article on membrane porosity and mass transport/permeation efficiency further emphasizes that porosity characteristics affect molecular transport and permeation efficiency [N3-R3]. Taken together, these sources support the conclusion that pore size distribution determines rejection by controlling the pathways available to solutes and by influencing the balance between sieving, transport, and adsorption [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3].

Hydraulic retention time and shear affect solute entry and retention. The 2023 MF/UF nanosphere study shows that fouling mechanisms and permeate flux behavior depend on operating pressures and that different pressures produce different fouling layers and rejection efficiencies [N5-F4]. It also reports that cake formed under 50 kPa had the lowest porosity but the best EDC removal efficiency, which may be attributed to adsorption and size exclusion [N5-F4]. This indicates that hydraulic conditions can change how much solute enters the membrane, how it is retained, and how efficiently it is removed. The 2013 UF study on EDC removal by membrane fouling reports that fouling behavior of humic compounds followed cake filtration, and that fouled UF membranes showed enhanced EDC removal by 0.0% to 58.3% for different EDCs [N1-F1]. The same paper states that EDC removal was mainly governed by hydrophobic adsorption until steady state, after which size exclusion became dominant [N1-F1]. These findings suggest that hydraulic retention time and shear influence the formation of fouling layers and the transition from adsorption-dominated to size-exclusion-dominated removal, with longer retention times potentially allowing more adsorption and cake formation, while shear may affect the stability of the fouling layer and the ease with which solutes can be retained [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Membrane material and surface charge influence retention and fouling. The 2023 UF study reports that fouling behavior of humic compounds obeyed cake filtration, and that fouled UF membranes showed enhanced EDC removal [N1-F1]. It also notes that hydrophobic interaction between EDCs and the membrane surface is unfavorable and limits rejection, but that fouling can enhance removal by forming a cake layer [N1-F1]. The 2026 NF study on hydrophobic EDCs reports that chlorinated membranes can suppress hydrophobic interaction and improve rejection, and that the chlorinated VNF1 membrane showed higher sorption but also higher rejection because increased sorption was offset by enhanced size exclusion [N4-F2]. The 2021 NF study on MoS2-integrated membranes similarly states that hydrophilic surface properties and selective nanochannels can reduce hydrophobic interaction and enhance rejection, and that the selective nanochannels played a more important role than hydrophilic surface in impeding transport of EDCs [N4-F3]. These examples show that membrane material and surface charge matter because they control hydrophobic interaction, adsorption, and fouling. In particular, hydrophilic surfaces and surface modifications can reduce hydrophobic interaction, thereby improving rejection and reducing fouling, while hydrophobic surfaces can enhance adsorption and fouling [N1-F1][N4-F2][N4-F3].

Overall, the evidence indicates that pore size cutoff and pore size distribution are central to separation by size, hydraulic retention time and shear affect solute entry and the transition from adsorption to size exclusion, and membrane material and surface charge determine whether EDCs are retained by adsorption, hydrophobic interaction, or size exclusion [N6-R2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N1-F1][N5-F4][N4-F2][N4-F3].

Adsorption mechanisms affect EDC removal and fouling behavior by determining which EDCs are adsorbed versus rejected, by changing adsorption capacity, affinity, and kinetics with pore size and surface properties, and by altering fouling layer structure and long-term membrane performance.

Which EDCs are adsorbed versus rejected by membrane surfaces and fouling layers depends on molecular properties and membrane chemistry. The 2023 NF study on hydrophobic EDC removal reports that hydrophobic EDCs are often neutral and hydrophobic [N4-F3], and that their removal is limited by unfavorable hydrophobic interaction with the membrane surface [N4-F3]. It also states that the introduction of hydrophilic surface features and selective nanochannels can reduce hydrophobic interaction and enhance rejection [N4-F3]. The 2026 NF study similarly reports that hydrophobic EDCs are strongly adsorbed, but that high sorption can reduce rejection because the compound can bypass the rejection layer at steady state [N4-F2]. These findings suggest that hydrophobic EDCs are more likely to be adsorbed onto membrane surfaces and fouling layers, whereas more hydrophilic or smaller EDCs are more likely to be rejected by size exclusion and other transport mechanisms [N4-F2][N4-F3]. The 2026 NF paper also notes that chlorinated membranes can suppress hydrophobic interaction and improve rejection, while the chlorinated VNF1 membrane showed higher sorption but also higher rejection because increased sorption was offset by enhanced size exclusion [N4-F2]. This indicates that adsorption is not the only fate of EDCs; some EDCs may be adsorbed initially, then retained in the fouling layer, and then rejected through transport or further adsorption [N4-F2][N4-F3].

Adsorption capacity, affinity, and kinetics change with pore size and surface properties. The 2023 NF study reports that hydrophobic EDCs are often neutral and hydrophobic, and that their removal is limited by unfavorable hydrophobic interaction with the membrane surface [N4-F3]. The 2026 NF study states that the chlorinated NF90 membrane exhibited significantly reduced sorption and enhanced rejection for EDCs, primarily because of enhanced hydrophilic carboxyl groups that suppressed hydrophobic interaction [N4-F2]. The same paper also reports that the chlorinated VNF1 membrane showed higher sorption but also higher rejection because increased sorption was offset by enhanced size exclusion [N4-F2]. These examples show that pore size and surface chemistry can alter adsorption capacity and affinity: hydrophilic surfaces reduce hydrophobic interaction, lowering adsorption and increasing rejection, whereas hydrophobic surfaces or pore structures that allow more surface contact may increase adsorption [N4-F2][N4-F3]. The 2023 NF study further notes that the developed MoS2-integrated membrane simultaneously enhanced permeance and EDC rejection, with water/EDC selectivity nearly 6 times larger than the control [N4-F3]. This suggests that surface modifications can change the kinetics of adsorption and transport, making rejection more selective and reducing fouling [N4-F3]. The 2021 NF study on MoS2-integrated membranes also emphasizes that selective nanochannels played a more important role than the hydrophilic surface in impeding EDC transport across the PA layer [N4-F3], showing that pore-scale structure can affect both adsorption and transport kinetics.

Adsorption alters fouling layer structure and long-term membrane performance. The 2013 UF study on EDC removal by membrane fouling reports that fouling behavior of humic compounds obeyed cake filtration and that fouled UF membranes showed enhanced EDC removal by 0.0% to 58.3% for different EDCs [N1-F1]. Membrane pore size and adsorption mechanisms are two central factors that determine the efficiency of ultrafiltration (UF) and microfiltration (MF) membranes in removing endocrine-disrupting compounds (EDCs). The evidence across the branch reports points to a complex interaction: pore size governs whether EDCs are rejected by size exclusion or can enter the membrane and be retained by transport or adsorption, while adsorption mechanisms determine which EDCs are more likely to be captured on membrane surfaces or fouling layers, and how that affects long-term membrane performance [N7][N8][N9][N10].

---

## 1) Pore size and membrane structure determine transport and rejection

Membrane pore size and pore size distribution are the primary determinants of solute separation by size. The branch report on pore size and membrane structure states that particles are rejected if they are larger than the UF/MF membrane pore size, and that pore size governs which particles pass through the membrane [N6-R2]. The 2023 MF/UF nanosphere study provides direct experimental evidence that MF membranes reject 120 nm polystyrene nanospheres at only 26%, while UF membranes show different fouling behavior depending on pore blocking and cake layer formation [N5-F4]. This supports the idea that pore size cutoff is not a simple binary threshold: it depends on the membrane’s pore size distribution, the particle size, and operating conditions [N5-F4].

Pore size distribution also affects transport and rejection. The branch report on pore size distribution in UF membranes notes that the impact of pore-size-distribution forms on UF membrane performance was investigated [N3-R1]. Although the evidence here is not detailed enough to specify the exact pore-size-distribution mechanisms, it clearly supports the broader idea that membrane performance is sensitive to how pore sizes are distributed across the membrane structure [N3-R1]. The 2000 study on determining pore size distributions of UF membranes by model calculations also examined the effects of protein adsorption on membrane transport and noted that different adsorption mechanisms lead to very different behavior [N3-R2]. This shows that pore size distribution is intertwined with transport, and that membrane structure can influence whether solutes are retained by sieving, transport, or adsorption [N3-R2].

Membrane material and surface charge also influence retention and fouling. The branch report on pore size and membrane structure reports that hydrophobic interaction between EDCs and the membrane surface is unfavorable and limits rejection, while fouling can enhance removal by forming a cake layer [N1-F1]. It also notes that membrane material and surface charge matter because they control hydrophobic interaction, adsorption, and fouling [N1-F1]. The 2026 NF study on hydrophobic EDCs reports that chlorinated membranes can suppress hydrophobic interaction and improve rejection, and that the chlorinated VNF1 membrane showed higher sorption but also higher rejection because increased sorption was offset by enhanced size exclusion [N4-F2]. The 2021 NF study on MoS2-integrated membranes similarly states that hydrophilic surface properties and selective nanochannels can reduce hydrophobic interaction and enhance rejection, and that selective nanochannels played a more important role than hydrophilic surface in impeding EDC transport across the PA layer [N4-F3]. Taken together, these findings show that membrane material and surface chemistry determine whether EDCs are retained by adsorption, hydrophobic interaction, or size exclusion [N1-F1][N4-F2][N4-F3].

Hydraulic retention time and shear affect solute entry and retention. The 2013 UF study on EDC removal by membrane fouling reports that fouling behavior of humic compounds obeyed cake filtration and that fouled UF membranes showed enhanced EDC removal by 0.0% to 58.3% for different EDCs [N1-F1]. Adsorption mechanisms determine which EDCs are adsorbed versus rejected by membrane surfaces and fouling layers. These findings suggest that hydrophobic EDCs are more likely to be adsorbed onto membrane surfaces and fouling layers, whereas more hydrophilic or smaller EDCs are more likely to be rejected by size exclusion and other transport mechanisms [N4-F2][N4-F3].

These findings indicate that pore size and fouling type strongly influence flux and rejection: pore blocking and cake formation can reduce flux, but they can also create different rejection environments that change how EDCs are retained over time [N5-F4][N1-F1].

---

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Overall, the evidence shows that membrane pore size and adsorption mechanisms interact in a nonlinear way to determine UF and MF efficiency for EDC removal. Pore size cutoff and pore size distribution separate solutes by size, but pore size distribution also affects transport and adsorption because it shapes the membrane structure and available pathways for solutes [N6-R2][N3-R1]. Hydraulic retention time and shear affect solute entry and retention, shifting the dominant rejection mechanism from adsorption to size exclusion as fouling develops [N5-F4][N1-F1]. Membrane material and surface charge influence retention and fouling by controlling hydrophobic interaction and adsorption [N1-F1][N4-F2][N4-F3].

Adsorption mechanisms determine which EDCs are adsorbed versus rejected, and they change with pore size and surface properties. Hydrophobic EDCs are often strongly adsorbed, but high sorption can reduce rejection because the compound can bypass the rejection layer at steady state [N4-F2]. Adsorption can temporarily improve removal by forming a cake layer, but sustained adsorption can reduce steady-state rejection and complicate long-term operation [N1-F1][N4-F3].

EDC physicochemistry determines which rejection mechanism dominates. Molecular weight, hydrophobicity, and charge are key determinants, with highly hydrophobic EDCs typically governed by adsorption and size exclusion, while charged or more hydrophilic EDCs may be governed by electrostatic repulsion and size exclusion [N9][N6-R1][N4-R5]. Solubility and diffusivity are especially important for small EDCs and when pore size is close to molecular dimensions, because those molecules may enter the membrane and then be rejected by transport limitations, size exclusion, or adsorption in the rejection layer [N6-R2][N4-F3].

Pore size-dependent rejection mechanisms differ across EDC classes and membrane types. Hydrophobic EDCs are mainly rejected by adsorption plus size exclusion, while charged or more hydrophilic EDCs may be mainly rejected by electrostatic repulsion and size exclusion [N10][N6-R1]. Pore size and rejection mechanism also affect long-term flux and fouling by shifting dominant rejection mechanisms and altering fouling layer structure [N1-F1][N5-F4].

---

## Bottom line

For UF and MF membranes, efficiency in removing EDCs depends on a combination of pore size, adsorption, physicochemical properties, and operating conditions. Smaller pores can exclude larger EDCs, but pore size distribution and membrane structure also control transport and adsorption. Hydrophobic EDCs are often adsorbed, but high sorption can reduce steady-state rejection. Adsorption can temporarily improve removal by forming a fouling cake, but sustained adsorption can reduce long-term performance. Charge and molecular weight determine which rejection mechanism dominates, with highly hydrophobic EDCs usually governed by adsorption and size exclusion, and charged EDCs by electrostatic repulsion and size exclusion. Pore size-dependent rejection mechanisms differ across EDC classes and membrane types, and they strongly influence long-term flux and fouling [N7][N8][N9][N10].
